text: Improved Molecular Assay for Sex Identification of the Endangered Crested Ibis (Nipponia nippon) Based on the CHD1 Gene and a Sex-linked Microsatellite Locus

Sex identification of monomorphic birds, especially endangered avian species, is essential for ecological study and biodiversity conservation. In this study, two popular primer sets of 2550F/2718R and P2/P8, which were designed to amplify different fragments of chromodomain-helicase-DNA binding protein 1 (CHD1) genes mapped on both Z and W chromosomes in birds, were used to identify for the first time the sex of individuals of the endangered species crested ibis (Nipponia nippon) in a large number of samples. An improved primer set of 2467F/2530R was re-designed to be specific to crested ibis following their conserved sequences derived from the 2550F/2718R primers. PCR products of the new primers were conveniently visualized with two bands of 552 base pairs (bp) and 358 bp for females, but a single band of 552 bp for males in routine 1.8% agarose gel. Similarly, the P2/P8 primer set amplified two fragments of 398 bp and 381 bp from females but one fragment of 398 bp from males; however, a high resolution involving 10% polyacrylamide gel had to be employed to resolve the 17 bp insertions/deletions (in/dels) present between the two amplicons in females. In addition, a microsatellite locus NnNF05 was validated to be sex-linked and shown to be effective in the sexing of crested ibis, supporting its utility in non-invasive sampling. This study provides a rapid, convenient, and reliable molecular assay for improving sex identification in the monomorphic and monogamous crested ibis, and thus facilitates the selection of breeding pairs in captive programs and reintroduction initiatives.

It is necessary to correctly identify sex for wildlife conservation as well as evolutionary and ecological studies (Miyaki et al., 1998;Birkhead et al., 2001;Dubiec et al., 2006). In avian species, females have heterogametic sex chromosomes Z and W, whereas male birds are homogametic ZZ (Ellegren, 2001). The sex chromosome-linked chromodomain-helicase-DNA binding protein (CHD1) gene is one of the universal targets for molecular sexing in birds (e.g., Ellegren, 1996;Griffiths et al., 1996). Two homologous CHD1 genes are mapped on each W or Z chromosome. They share relatively conserved exons while carrying highly polymorphic introns, often in different nucleotide lengths between the two genes. These structural differences allow the clear differentiation of PCR amplicons from homologous fragments of the CHD1-W and CHD1-Z genes; however, the level of homology between different fragments of the two genes varies among bird species (e.g., Kahn et al., 1998). Primer sets such as 2550F/2718R (Fridolfsson and Ellegren, 1999), P2/P8 (Griffiths et al., 1998) and 1237L/1272H (Kahn et al., 1998) were subsequently designed to target different introns of the two genes, of which the latter two sets were found to flank the same intron (Jensen et al., 2003). Sex identification with a microsatellite locus, which requires a only minimal amount of template DNA, which can often be recovered from shed feathers, fecal samples, or historical specimens, is appropriate for non-invasive sampling, as has been reported in several bird species, such as whooping crane (Jones and Glenn, 1999) and falcon (Nesje and Røed, 2000).
The crested ibis (Nipponia nippon) is monogamous, and since 2000 has been listed as "Endangered" in the IUCN Red List of Threatened Species (BirdLife International, 2012). With the continuous conservation efforts made since the rediscovery of a remnant wild population in China in 1981, the population of crested ibis has increased both in the wild and in captivity (Zhang and Ding, 2008;Ding, 2004Ding, , 2010)). However, as a phenotypically monomorphic bird spe-cies, mistakes were sometimes made during the selection of breeding pairs for captive and reintroduction program. A sufficient and convenient method is needed to correctly identify the gender of individuals of this species at different ages. In the present study, the primer sets of 2550F/2718R and P2/ P8 were tested and then improved for sex identification of crested ibis. In addition, a sex-linked microsatellite locus NnNF05 was validated for non-invasive sampling.

Blood samples from 33 crested ibis individuals whose sexes were known from management records (20 males and 13 females) were collected from the Shaanxi Crested Ibis Captive Breeding Center, Yangxian County, Shaanxi Province, China in 2010. The blood samples were collected from wing vein and mixed with an equal volume of anticoagulant buffer (0.1 M Tris-Cl, 0.1 M EDTA and 1% SDS, pH 8.0). All the samples were stored at -80°C. Total genomic DNA was extracted following a conventional phenol/chloroform protocol (Sambrook and Russell, 2001). After qualification and quantification using a NenoDrop-1000 spectrophotometer (NanoDrop Technologies Inc., Wilmington, USA), the DNAs were diluted with TE buffer to around 100 ng/μl and stored at -20°C.

section: amplification of chd1 gene fragments using previously reported primers
text: Six individuals with relatively large quantity of genomic DNAs (three females and three males) were selected to test the effectiveness of PCR amplifications using the two primer sets of 2550F/ 2718R and P2/P8 with detailed sequences as reported in Fridolfsson and Ellegren (1999) and Griffiths et al. (1998), respectively. The amplification was performed in 20 μl volume containing around 50 ng DNA, 0.75 units of Taq DNA polymerase (Tiangen Biotech Co., Ltd., China), 2 μl of 10× Taq buffer, 2 μl of dNTPs (2.5 mM) and 0.3 μl each of the forward and reverse primers (10 pmol/μl). To optimize the PCR conditions, a gradient PCR program involving temperatures ranging from 50°C to 62°C was employed using a T Gradient thermal cycler (Biometra, Göttingen, Germany). The final thermal cycling was performed using a GeneAmp PCR system 9700 thermal cycler (Applied Biosystems, Foster City, CA, USA) started with 5 min at 94°C, and followed by 30 cycles of 40 s at 94°C, 30 s at 55°C (2550F/2718R) or 52°C (P2/P8) and 30 s at 72°C, and finished by a final extension of 7 min at 72°C. The PCR products in 3.5 μl each were resolved by 1.8% agarose gel electrophoresis containing Gold View TM Nucleic Acid Stain (SBS Genetech Co., Ltd, China) to confirm their quality and quantity. Three microliters of denatured PCR products of P2/P8 were further loaded in 10% nondenaturing polyacrylamide gel (Acr:Bis = 29:1) for 12-14 h electrophoresis in 1× TBE buffer at 4°C and 160 V, and the gel was silver stained for visualization.

section: direct sequencing and cloning of the pcr products and redesigning of primers for chd1 genes
text:
Two strong bands around 450 bp and 650 bp each of the PCR products from one female while a single strong band around 650 bp from a male amplified with the 2550F/2718R primers (Fig. 1) were purified and then directly sequenced by the BigDye ® Terminator v3.1 Cycle Sequencing Kit (Applied Biosystems) involving the two PCR primers.
Based on the conserved regions inside the 2550F/2718Rderived sequences (their designations were determined based on the 5′-primer sequence nucleotide of a full length murine (Mus musculus) CHD1 mRNA sequence; Delmas et al., 1993;Fridolfsson and Ellegren, 1999), a pair of crested ibis specific primers (2467F: 5′-CGT CAG TTT CCC TTT CAG-3′ and 2530R: 5′-CCA GTG CTT GTT TCC TCA-3′; primer designations were scored according to a complete chicken Gallus gallus CHD1 mRNA sequence with a GenBank accession number of AB465210; Okada et al., 2009) was re-designed and then applied to all individuals following the same PCR conditions but with an annealing temperature at 52°C.
The PCR product of a male bird amplified using P2/P8 primers was purified and then directly sequenced using the two PCR primers, following the same procedure as described for the 2550F/ 2718R primers. The two PCR products from a female were ligated into a pMD 18-T vector (TaKaRa, China) and transformed into DH5α-competent cells. The clones were cultured overnight on LB/ Ampicillin/IPTG/X-gal plates for blue/white selection and the positive clones were further confirmed by PCR amplification with universal primers of M13-47 and M13-48. A total of 10 positive clones were sequenced using the two M13 primers.
The raw sequencing data was manually edited using Chromas version 2.23 (http://www.technelysium.om.au/chromas,html) and aligned with MEGA5 software (Tamura et al., 2011).

All 19 polymorphic microsatellite loci without chromosome assignments of crested ibis (Ji et al., 2004;He et al., 2006) were included in this study to screen for possible sex-linked marker(s) following similar PCR conditions. The denatured PCR products were loaded into a non-denaturing polyacrylamide gel, as described for P2/P8 PCR products. Microsatellite locus showing different conformations of males from females was chosen for genotyping using a fluorescent-labeled forward primer at its 5′-end and an ABI 3130xl Genetic Analyzer (Applied Biosystems) for all the samples.

Molecular sexing involving the two previously reported primer sets for all 33 crested ibis was found to be in complete agreement with their management records, confirming the utility of these primers. However, the 2550F/2718R set showed some non-specific PCR amplifications apart from the two expected bands of approximately 450 bp and 650 bp with relatively high intensities (Fig. 1). The newly designed primers of 2467F/2530R significantly improved the PCR specificity for crested ibis. The reduced PCR products by 105 bp enhanced the relative size contract between the two PCR amplicons with easy and clear resolution in routine 1.8% agarose gel (Fig. 2; left). All females had two PCR products of 552 bp and 358 bp (the two sequences were submitted to GenBank with accession numbers of KC545379 and KC545380) while males shared a single The PCR amplification with P2/P8 primers was found to be specific and non-polymorphic for either sex across all samples (Fig. 2; right); however, the two amplicons of 398 bp and 381 bp each (the cloned sequences were submitted to GenBank with accession numbers of KC545381 and KC545382) from females had to be resolved using a 10% polyacrylamide gel (Fig. 3) for their limited 17 bp in/dels. The males only shared the 398 bp PCR amplicon.
Alignment of the four new crested ibis sequences generated with 2550F/2718R and P2/P8 primer sets against both complete mRNA sequence (AB465210) and spliced genomic DNA sequence of chicken CHD1-Z gene (between 6,228,619-6,273,882 in NW_003764319.1; Bellott et al., 2010) as well as the homologous partial CHD1-W gene (since the 8th exon in NW_003766117; International Chicken Genome Sequencing Consortium, 2004) using the Splign program (Kapustin et al., 2008) identified highly homologous regions in the chicken CHD1-Z and CHD1-W genes. We confirmed that these two primer sets target two different introns, the former spanning the 16th and 17th exons (Fig. 4A) while the latter crossing the 22nd and 23rd exons (Fig. 4B). Further BLAST query of the 552 bp and 358 bp-long sequences against the GenBank nucleotide collections identified their high homology with the partial CHD1-Z (AY464013, 96%) and CHD1-W (AY464014, 98%) genes of black-faced spoonbill (Platalea minor; Cheng et al., 2006). The BLAST results also demonstrated that the complete long fragment (398 bp) from the P2/P8 primers was similar (90% identify) to the homologous portion of Indian vulture (Gyps indicus) CHD1-Z gene (HQ236387; Ghorpade et al., 2012) while the short fragment (381 bp) was close (94% identity) to the homologous portion of Magellanic penguin (Spheniscus magellanicus) CHD1-W gene (GU451239; Zhang et al., 2012). Taken together, these suggest the wellconserved nature of the homologous CHD1-Z and CHD1-W gene fragments across avian species.
Only one microsatellite locus, NnNF05, showed different conformations between males and females in polyacrylamide gel documentation. Based on the sequence of a cloned NnNF05 fragment (AJ699416; Ji et al., 2004), a new pair of PCR primers (NnNF05Fa: 5′-TGA AGG CAG GTG GAG AAG T-3′ and NnNF05Ra: 5′-TAT GCA GCT GAG GAG GAG A-3′) was re-designed to amplify a relatively small fragment around 170 bp that was genotyped using the Genetic Analyzer. The genotyping data illustrated that all the females had two alleles in 172 bp and 169 bp, while all males only shared the 172 bp allele.

Accurate sexing provides critical information for population structure monitoring which involves sex ratio data, as well as for the selection of mating pairs in any effective conservation program. Steroid sexing and karyotyping are either unreliable or time-consuming (Malagó Jr et al., 2002;von Engelhardt and Groothuis, 2005) while laparoscopy could be harmful and even lethal to some birds. For these same reasons, these methods are unsuitable for sex determination in crested ibis. Several previous studies on the molecular sex identification of crested ibis (Itoh et al., 2001;Li et al., 2001;Park et al., 2011;Kasuga et al., 2012) were all based on PCR amplifications involving different primer combinations targeting the same single fragment of W-linked EE0.6 sequence that was cloned from Oriental white stork (Itoh et al., 1997) and chicken (Ogawa et al., 1997). However, a correct identification of this EE0.6 fragment from crested ibis required a duplex PCR involving species specific primers (Park et al., 2011;Kasuga et al., 2012) as well as an internal control, e.g., the conserved exon of common W and Z chromosome-linked spindlin gene (Itoh et al., 2001) or the mitochondrial 12S rRNA gene (Park et al., 2011), to exclude possible false negatives due to technical failure (Itoh et al., 2001).
The P2/P8 has been a commonly used primer set for sex identification in avian species (e.g., Griffiths, et al., 1998;Jensen et al., 2003;Cerit and Avanus, 2007); however, length differences between the CHD1-Z and CHD1-W introns were found to be varied among species and it may be necessary to use a polyacrylamide gel if such differences are to be limited (e.g., Miyaki et al., 1998;Dawson et al., 2001;Jensen et al., 2003). The length polymorphisms of CHD1-Z introns and thus resultant heterozygous CHD1-Z alleles, as found in male upland sandpiper (Bartramia longicauda), can certainly complicate the interpretation of PCR amplifications (Casey et al., 2009). When these primers were first applied to crested ibis (Kim et al., 2012), two PCR products each of CHD1-Z and CHD1-W genes around 400 bp and 380 bp, respectively, were generated and proved to be very difficult to separate, even in 3% agarose gel. The products were further sequenced for the development of a duplex PCR involving two forward (pci1 and pci2) and one reverse (pci3) primers targeting two shorter fragments of 233 bp for CHD1-Z (AB620020.1) and 129 bp for CHD1-W (AB620021.1) genes, which were nearly identical to the two longer homologous P2/P8 sequences obtained in this study. The nonpolymorphic nature of either CHD1-Z or CHD1-W fragment among large number of samples nevertheless validated the utility of the P2/P8 primers in the sexing of crested ibis.
Kikuchi and Ishii (2002) adopted the P1/ P2 primers (Griffiths et al., 1996) for PCR amplification and cloning of two very short sequences from crested ibis, 64 bp each of the CHD1-W (AB049443.1) and of CHD1-Z (AB049444.1) genes, which were completely identical to our partial P2/P8 sequences located within the 23rd exon carrying three SNPs. Two of these SNPs were subsequently selected for the development of PCR-RFLPs for sex identification. However, digestion with HaeIII and MboII enzymes of PCR products from males were incomplete, making the discrimination of such digestions between males and females difficult, necessitating the use of a 6% or 8% polyacrylamide gel to resolve such small digested products. Alignment of the P1 primer sequence against to our P2/P8 sequences identified one or two nucleotide mismatches to the crested ibis CHD1-Z or CHD1-W gene, confirming the presence of non-specific amplifications of such short fragments by the P1/P2 primers (Kikuchi and Ishii, 2002).
As shown in our data, the size difference of the 16th intron was much larger than that of the 22nd intron between CHD1-Z and CHD1-W genes in most bird species. Therefore, a pair of crested ibis specific primers, the 2467F/2530R flanking the 16th intron, was re-designed in this study based on the conserved DNA sequences of partial CHD1-Z and CHD1-W genes first generated using the 2550F/2718R primers that were originally designed following the cDNA sequencing of chicken CHD1-W and CHD1-Z genes (Ellegren and Fridolfsson, 1997;Fridolfsson and Ellegren, 1999). When the oligonucleotides of the four primers were aligned to available homologous genomic DNA sequences in CHD1-W and CHD1-Z genes of different bird species (Fig. 5), the original 2550F/2718R primers showed a few mismatches across species or between these two genes in the same species, and were thus expected to lead to nonspecific amplifications, as was observed in the case of crested ibis, or even to allele drop out or null alleles (Robertson and Gemmell, 2006;Kasuga et al., 2012). The 2467F/2530R also had similar levels of mismatches across these species; thus, the concept of developing 'universal primers' for sexing different bird species must be approached cautiously (Griffiths et al., 1998;Fridolfsson and Ellegren, 1999;Dawson et al., 2001;Jensen et al., 2003;Casey et al., 2009).
In conclusion, the P2/P8 primers flanking the 22nd intron were further validated for their utility in sex identification in crested ibis, but the limited size difference of two PCR products in females complicated their discrimination. The redesigned 2467F/2530R primers targeting its 16th intron of both CHD1-Z and CHD1-W genes of crested ibis only involved a single PCR reaction with a single amplicon in males or two amplicons in females with a size difference in 194 bp within the 16th intron, which can be easily virtualized in routine agarose gel. The detection of the sex-linked microsatellite locus of NnNF05 offered an option for molecular sexing through fluorescence genotyping, which is thought to be appropriate when dealing with non-invasive samples and can also be integrated into multiplex PCRs with other microsatellite loci for population genetic studies (Jones and Glenn, 1999;Dubiec and Zagalska-Neubauer, 2006). All three sets of primers (2467F/2530R, P2/P8 and NnNF05) generated smaller PCR products from the W than from the Z alleles, ensuring the detection of W alleles following a probable preferential amplification. Therefore these primers may offer advantages in avoiding the potential problem of mistyping females as males. It is expected that the improved molecular assay for sex identification validated and developed in this study will facilitate further studies on the behavior and population ecology as well as breeding management of crested ibis.
